lesson.menu_desc: Indirect requests -- Would you mind / I was wondering if you could -- and how to say no politely -- 28 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 23 — Making and Responding to Requests
lesson.title_tag: Professor View — Vanessa Giuriati | Lesson 23 — Making and Responding to Requests
lesson.grammar_point: indirect requests (Would you mind + -ing / I was wondering if you could)

listenings.text: There is one rule about asking for things in English that nobody teaches you, and it is almost mathematical. The longer the request, the softer it sounds. Send me the report is four words and it feels like an order. Could you send me the report is six, and it is fine with almost anyone. Would you mind sending me the report is seven, and now the other person can say no without any drama. I was wondering if you could send me the report is eleven words, and you would only use it for something big, or with somebody who is already swamped. Notice what the long versions actually do. They do not make you weaker. They give the other person a way out. And that is exactly why people say yes. A request with no exit is not a request, it is an instruction, and instructions are for machines.

I used to be terrible at saying no. I would go quiet for two days and hope the person forgot, which is the worst possible answer. Then a colleague gave me a formula, and I have used it ever since. Three parts. First, say no early. A fast no is a kindness; a slow no wastes somebody's week. Second, give one reason, not four. I am swamped until Thursday is enough. When you give four reasons, it sounds like you are looking for permission. Third, offer something small. I cannot join the whole workshop, but I can review the slides on Friday. That last part is what keeps the door open. And here is the thing nobody expects: when you turn people down clearly, they trust your yes more. If you never refuse anything, nobody knows what your yes is worth.

extra_audio.text: First, I check whether it is a good moment: sorry to bother you, do you have a minute? Then I name the situation honestly, including the fact that it is short notice. After that, I make the request the long way round: I was wondering if you could take the call. Next, I give the other person a way out: if you are swamped, just turn me down. In the end, I say thank you and I admit that I owe them one.
